Lessons.Title: Estimate and Measure Weight
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Illustrative Mathematics Grade3 Unit6 Lesson6 aligns CCSS 3.MD.A.2 and introduces GRAMS and KILOGRAMS as units of WEIGHT. Public teacher lesson.html SHA256 f558afcf987db0da134a7722c160fd27b3a9fdc9585682f29bf60a49185370e1 and preparation.html SHA256 ac934d245ddfec9fb1bd156f294ef31e79bc5674b1ca35c4df72c4dbfc882d26 were reviewed in the owner-device local archive. Source student-facing text covers original produce-stand warm-up, five weight benchmarks and four sorting bands, and four pets matched to four weight choices. The original separately formatted student PDF and copyrighted photographs have not been inspected; source semantics only, not image/pixel parity.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: Produce Stand (10 minutes) shows a fruit/vegetable stall with a person at work. Students may mention different types of produce or ask about prices, but source teacher's mathematical focus is that weight is a measurable attribute used, for example, when pricing produce or assessing how heavy something is. Several observations and questions are valid; do not turn this original open warm-up into one automatically graded answer.

Activity1 Estimate Weight (30 minutes) teaches familiar benchmarks: a source photo describes a PAPER CLIP as approximately ONE GRAM; a BASKET OF APPLES as approximately ONE KILOGRAM. The lesson gives exactly FIVE physical weights for students to hold:1 gram,10 grams,100 grams,1 kilogram,2 kilograms. The teacher prepares examples, dividing class into FIVE groups which rotate objects in approximately TWO-MINUTE turns until each group has handled all five weights. Pupils propose ANY reasonable items that would feel about as heavy as each original benchmark; do not demand one fixed object or say these estimates are certified scale readings.

The 2021 teacher preparation gives examples of a one-gram benchmark as a large paper clip, and an approximate one-kilogram setup as a filled 1-liter water bottle or teacher-made collection of paper clips. These are informal tactile benchmarks, not a claim that all water containers or paper clips universally have an exact specified weight. When a scale or balance is AVAILABLE, teacher may check selected estimated weights; scales and balances are optional in this lesson, not a source-mandated exact measurement for every object.

Activity1 source pupil task 1 requires students to give approximate same-weight examples separately for ALL FIVE listed benchmarks: 1 gram,10 grams,100 grams,1 kilogram,2 kilograms. Pupil task 2 has a FOUR-COLUMN classroom sort: objects LESS THAN 1 gram; BETWEEN 1 gram and 100 grams; BETWEEN 100 grams and1 kilogram; MORE THAN1 kilogram. Chosen objects and estimates are variable; teacher checks reasonableness and correct relation to boundary values. Do not automatically put a value EXACTLY 1 gram, exactly100 grams, or exactly1 kilogram into a strict 'between' interval without first clarifying interval boundary conventions with teacher.

Activity2 The Weight of Pets (10 minutes): ORIGINAL photographed pet labels are guinea pig, dog, small fish, cat; ORIGINAL four numerical cards are 20 kilograms,1 kilogram,3 kilograms,3 grams. Natural one-to-one grade-three intended REASONABLE estimate: guinea pig about1 kilogram, dog about20 kilograms, small fish about3 grams, cat about3 kilograms. These are photographic toy-category matching estimates rather than measured factual weights of particular animals; a specific pet's real mass can vary enormously. Teacher checks that pupil's chosen match is plausible and explanation uses size, units and first-hand earlier benchmarks; do not claim actual image pet weight was determined or factually weighed.

Source differentiation uses the measured weights physically from Activity1 again to help children justify pet-scale choices. MLR8 promotes words gram, kilogram and weight in paired explanations. Lesson synthesis asks when ESTIMATING instead of exactly measuring weight is useful: carrying an object, assessing a purchase, or reasoning informally. The local source uses the grade-three word weight without teaching weight-versus-mass distinction, which the source preparation explicitly says is outside scope.

Publisher Cool-down About a Kilogram is teacher-login restricted, and the publisher produce-market/paper-clip/apple/pet photographs have separate attribution and are not copied into Edulytics. Original pupil PDF, all seven image source files, tests, Stage D, academic approval, runtime rendering and production deployment remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Gram benchmark
KeyConcepts.Definition: A gram is a small metric weight unit familiar from a paper-clip-sized reference object.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use gram scale for light objects and compare to tactile 1g/10g/100g examples.
KeyConcepts.Example: An individual paper clip is roughly one gram in the original source.

KeyConcepts.Title: Kilogram benchmark
KeyConcepts.Definition: A kilogram is a much larger metric weight unit for heavier objects.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use kilograms for heavier items; use tactile1kg/2kg benchmarks.
KeyConcepts.Example: A basket of apples in the original source represents about one kilogram.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate, then verify if possible
KeyConcepts.Definition: A weight estimate is a reasoned approximate comparison, not a scale reading.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Propose plausible mass range; use a scale or balance if the original teacher has one available.
KeyConcepts.Example: A pet dog might plausibly be assigned20kg from four provided source cards.

KeyConcepts.Title: Boundary reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: Weight categories compare to 1g,100g,1kg and may be open about endpoints.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check strict less-than/more-than and ask teacher what 'between' includes at exact boundaries.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match five physical benchmarks
WorkedExamples.Question: What source reference weights must each group get a chance to hold?
WorkedExamples.Method: List all original objects in the teacher's rotation.
WorkedExamples.Check: FIVE source weights, approximate two-minute turn for each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Paper clip and apple basket source pictures
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is the smaller source weight?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare typical gram and kilogram reference units.
Steps: Basket is considerably heavier, but real object sizes vary.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source images are illustrations, not precise weight scale readings.

WorkedExamples.Title: Pet match using source choices
WorkedExamples.Question: Use each original numerical card for a reasonable matching pet.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use source-grade weight sense and physical size.
WorkedExamples.Check: Intended estimate only, not actual specific animal weight.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish an estimation from a measurement
WorkedExamples.Question: If no scale is available, can the exact weight of a classroom object be confirmed?
WorkedExamples.Method: Discuss human approximation and optional instrument verification.
Steps: Say it is an estimate until measured on a suitable scale.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No exact measured value without measurement
WorkedExamples.Check: The original source allows optional scale demonstration only.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say five classroom benchmark weights are exact real weights of the photographic objects.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source uses approximate paperclip/apple images as anchors for estimating.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record about 1g/about1kg; distinguish known teacher-supplied weights from typical object pictures.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a 20kg pet weight as guaranteed for every dog.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The assignment is match a COULD BE weight, not measure the pictured animal.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Grade plausibility in the original four-choice task and request explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Require a fixed classroom object per weight range.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Student independently chooses objects and estimates; many valid examples.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks actual examples against source boundary categories.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Force all children to use a scale in the first lesson.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Teacher source says scale or balance IF available for synthesis; tactile reference is core.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up Produce Stand: multiple notice/wonder responses, weight as measurable attribute.
Activity1 five reference weights:1g,10g,100g,1kg,2kg; five rotating groups, two minutes per weight; student examples open.
Classroom objects sorted into four original weight bands with teacher-checked real choices.
Activity2 four original pets and cards: guinea pig1kg,dog20kg,small fish3g,cat3kg are plausible original matching choices, not actual measured weights.
Source uses term weight, not weight-versus-mass distinctions, and treats scales optional.
Original photographs, independent student PDF and publisher gated cooldown not verified; tests and Stage D unrun.
